I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

There is something about me that made the event happen

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette: When Dr. Malik first saw him in the intake room, the 44‑year‑old South‑Eastern Asian man—his name was Arun—looked weary, his eyes darting back and forth as if he were already mapping the hallway outside the clinic. He had been a registered nurse for fifteen years, a calm presence in the busy emergency department, but the mugging he had endured two years earlier had left a permanent echo behind him. On the morning of that night, Arun was walking home from the hospital, the fluorescent glow of the streetlights washing over his shoulders. He had been carrying a heavy tote of medical supplies when a figure emerged from a shadowed alley, thrust a bag over his shoulders, and demanded his wallet. The robber, unmasked but aggressive, had slammed his face into Arun’s, forcing him to stumble into a puddle of cold, dark water. The impact of the bag against his chest, the sudden surge of terror, the metallic taste of blood in his mouth—these were the core moments that Arun would replay with a clarity that felt almost photographic. He told the therapist that each time he closes his eyes, the image unfurls in front of him as if it were a photo, every detail sharp: the slick black clothing of the assailant, the hiss of the wind, the echoing crunch of his own shoes on wet asphalt. When the memory surfaces, he says, his body aches in the same spot he felt during the assault—the lower back and shoulders—an unbidden pain that rattles his bones as if the assault were happening again. Arun’s negative appraisal of the world has been a relentless undertone in his life since that night. “Nothing good can happen to me anymore,” he says, his voice low. “It feels like I brought this on myself. I’m not safe, I’m broken, and I have no future.” These beliefs have seeded his strategies and perceptions. He has begun to stare compulsively at every reflective surface, convinced that an unseen eye might be watching him. At the break room, he pauses, lifts his face to the metal mirror on the wall, and rechecks his own reflection for the slightest sign of danger. He keeps his mind busy all the time, humming a repetitive melody to keep the intrusive images at bay, and constantly scans his surroundings as if an invisible threat could materialize at any moment. The fear that “nothing good can happen” pushes him to sit only in the most shielded corners of the staff lounge, choosing the seat that feels the most protected, as if a seat could block a future attack. These coping behaviors are not merely idle rituals; they are a direct consequence of his core belief that he is flawed and doomed. The sense of threat is inescapable in Arun’s everyday work environment. While on the night shift, he will check behind each corridor twice before stepping forward, always looking for the silhouette of a potential assailant in the dim lighting. He avoids the hallway that runs beside the psychiatric wing because he imagines an unrecognizable face lurking behind the flickering fluorescent tubes. The constant threat of being followed or re‑victimized has tightened his mind’s loop: the more he feels unsafe, the more he scans; the more he scans, the more he perceives threat. When he walks past the emergency department’s high‑contrast posters, the bright colors flash, and he feels a surge of panic that makes his heart race as though the danger is immediate. That panic is the trigger that sends his memory back to that night, and the memory’s vividness feeds his belief that “nothing good can happen.” The memory’s re‑experience is so intense that he reports physical pain in the same areas where the assailant had struck, reinforcing the belief that his body remains a battlefield. Arun’s maladaptive strategies also reinforce his negative appraisals. Each time he mirrors himself, he focuses on his weary eyes, his hollow expression, as evidence of his fault. When he checks his environment, he often finds nothing, but the absence of threat only makes him more convinced that the danger is ever‑present. The mental distraction he uses to block the image fails to give him relief; instead, it reminds him that his mind is occupied by thoughts that threaten his peace. This constant vigilance, the constant re‑checking of his surroundings, keeps the memory fresh and vivid, making it hard for him to sleep. He reports trouble falling asleep, and when he does, he wakes repeatedly, the night’s darkness seeming as hostile as the streetlights of that fateful night. Each restless night amplifies his belief that he has no future and that he will never feel safe. The cycle has crept into his marriage as well. His wife, Nisha, watches him retreat into himself, the way he refuses to sit beside her at the dinner table because the kitchen light makes him feel exposed. She has tried to suggest counseling, but Arun insists that his fears are justified, that he must keep his guard up to avoid another loss. He has begun to avoid calling in for overtime shifts, fearing that a late shift might expose him to random danger. That avoidance has cost him a promotion he was about to receive, a consequence that has further reinforced his hopelessness. Arun’s decision to seek help came after a particularly harrowing night shift where he stared at his reflection in a vending machine, feeling as if a pair of eyes were watching him from inside his own body. He realized that his coping strategies had begun to control his life, that he was living in constant terror and that his job, his marriage, and his sense of self were all in jeopardy. What he fears most is that he will never feel safe again, that he will never sleep without the memory’s pain. What he hopes for is a way to quiet the relentless scan, to reclaim his nights, and to believe that a future with stability and joy is possible.
